claim: Mechanical forces play a critical role in tendon development and function, influencing cell behavior through mechanotransduction signaling pathways and subsequent extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling.
source: Mechanical forces play a critical role in tendon development and function, influencing cell behavior through mechanotransduction signaling pathways and subsequent extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about mechanical forces in tendon biology.

claim: Embryonic tendons show dramatic changes in expression of matrix remodeling associated 5b (mxra5b), matrilin 1 (matn1), and the transcription factor kruppel-like factor 2a (klf2a), as muscles start to contract.
source: Embryonic tendons show dramatic changes in expression of matrix remodeling associated 5b (mxra5b), matrilin 1 (matn1), and the transcription factor kruppel-like factor 2a (klf2a), as muscles start to contract.
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript showing differential expression of these genes.

claim: Muscle contractile forces influence the spatial and temporal expression patterns of mxra5b, matn1, and klf2a.
source: Using embryos paralyzed either by loss of muscle contractility or neuromuscular stimulation we confirm that muscle contractile forces influence the spatial and temporal expression patterns of all three genes.
evidence: This is confirmed through paralysis experiments using cacnb1 mutants and aBTX injections.

claim: Gene expression responses of mxra5b, matn1, and klf2a depend on force intensity, duration, and tissue stiffness.
source: Quantification of these gene expression changes across tenocytes at multiple tendon entheses and myotendinous junctions reveals that their responses depend on force intensity, duration, and tissue stiffness.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative isHCR data showing differential responses across different tendon types and force conditions.

claim: Force-responsive cellular mechanisms have been implicated in cell differentiation.
source: Force-responsive cellular mechanisms have been implicated in cell differentiation (D'Angelo et al., 2011), morphogenesis (Hamada, 2015; Keller et al., 2008), tissue maintenance and repair (Riley et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Force-responsive cellular mechanisms have been implicated in morphogenesis.
source: Force-responsive cellular mechanisms have been implicated in cell differentiation (D'Angelo et al., 2011), morphogenesis (Hamada, 2015; Keller et al., 2008), tissue maintenance and repair (Riley et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Force-responsive cellular mechanisms have been implicated in tissue maintenance and repair.
source: Force-responsive cellular mechanisms have been implicated in cell differentiation (D'Angelo et al., 2011), morphogenesis (Hamada, 2015; Keller et al., 2008), tissue maintenance and repair (Riley et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Tenocytes constantly remodel the surrounding ECM to adapt to contractile forces from muscles.
source: Tendons experience a broad range of contractile forces from muscles, such as extreme stretching forces on the human Achilles tendon during exercise, and their constitutive fibroblast populations (called tenocytes) constantly remodel the surrounding ECM to adapt (Subramanian and Schilling, 2015; Wang, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Myotendinous junctions at the vertical myosepta of developing somites form via distinct tendon-independent and -dependent stages.
source: For example, in the embryonic zebrafish trunk, myotendinous junctions (MTJs) at the vertical myosepta (VMS) of developing somites form via distinct tendon-independent and -dependent stages (Subramanian and Schilling, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In the tendon-independent phase, myofibers differentiate and secrete ECM proteins such as Thbs4b that localize to the pre-tendon ECM and mediate initial fiber attachment.
source: In the tendon-independent phase, myofibers differentiate and secrete ECM proteins such as Thbs4b that localize to the pre-tendon ECM and mediate initial fiber attachment.
evidence: This describes a specific developmental process based on prior knowledge.

claim: In response to muscle contraction, TPCs differentiate into mature tenocytes and extend long microtubule-rich processes laterally into the surrounding ECM of the VMS.
source: Later, in response to muscle contraction, TPCs differentiate into mature tenocytes and extend long microtubule-rich processes laterally into the surrounding ECM of the VMS, with which they regulate ECM composition locally in response to force (McNeilly et al., 1996; Pingel et al., 2014; Subramanian et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Contractile forces acting on MTJs activate transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) signaling in TPCs.
source: Contractile forces acting on these MTJs activate transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) signaling in TPCs (Berthet et al., 2013; Pryce et al., 2009; Subramanian et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TGF-β induces expression of the transcription factors Scleraxis (Scx) and Mohawk (Mkx), which drive tenocyte fate by directly promoting transcription of collagens enriched in tendon ECM.
source: Although not necessary for TPC specification, TGF-β induces expression of the transcription factors Scleraxis (Scx) and Mohawk (Mkx), which drive tenocyte fate by directly promoting transcription of collagens (i.e. Col1a1, Col1a2, Col12a1, and Col14) enriched in tendon ECM (Berthet et al., 2013; Maeda et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The enthesis region where a tendon attaches to cartilage or bone is structurally graded in stiffness with fibrocartilage closer to the bone.
source: For example, the enthesis region where a tendon attaches to cartilage or bone is structurally graded in stiffness with fibrocartilage closer to the bone.
evidence: This is established knowledge about enthesis structure.

claim: Fibrocartilage cells co-express Scx and Sox9, both direct transcriptional regulators of collagens.
source: Fibrocartilage cells co-express Scx and Sox9, both direct transcriptional regulators of collagens, and muscle activity regulates the ratio of their expression levels (Blitz et al., 2013; Subramanian et al., 2023; Zelzer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Muscle activity regulates the ratio of Scx and Sox9 expression levels in fibrocartilage cells.
source: Fibrocartilage cells co-express Scx and Sox9, both direct transcriptional regulators of collagens, and muscle activity regulates the ratio of their expression levels (Blitz et al., 2013; Subramanian et al., 2023; Zelzer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Muscle contraction is required for embryonic tenocyte maturation, morphogenesis and ECM production in zebrafish tendons in vivo.
source: We have also shown that muscle contraction is required for embryonic tenocyte maturation, morphogenesis and ECM production in zebrafish tendons in vivo (Subramanian et al., 2018; Subramanian and Schilling, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Differential expression analysis revealed 2788 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between twitching (36 hpf) and free-swimming (48 hpf) stages with p-value <0.05.
source: Differential expression analysis revealed 2788 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between twitching and free-swimming stages with p-value <0.05 (Figure 1E; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Known tenocyte markers such as tnmd, mkxa, and egr1 were upregulated at swimming stage (48 hpf).
source: These included known tenocyte markers such as tnmd, mkxa, and egr1 upregulated at swimming (Figure 1E, F), confirming that many of the sorted mCherry+ cells were tenocytes or TPCs.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: col2a1a and col9a1a, which are typically associated with cartilage development and morphogenesis, were among the top DEGs.
source: Surprisingly, these included col2a1a and col9a1a, which are typically associated with cartilage development and morphogenesis (Figure 1F) suggesting that an early subset of scxa+ cells in embryonic tendons are specified as developing enthesis cells (Subramanian et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1F and inference about enthesis cell specification.

claim: An early subset of scxa+ cells in embryonic tendons are specified as developing enthesis cells.
source: Surprisingly, these included col2a1a and col9a1a, which are typically associated with cartilage development and morphogenesis (Figure 1F) suggesting that an early subset of scxa+ cells in embryonic tendons are specified as developing enthesis cells (Subramanian et al., 2023).
evidence: This is inferred from the expression of cartilage-associated genes in scxa+ cells and supported by a citation.

claim: Dual-expressing scxa/sox9a+ cells localize to cartilage attachment sites of cranial muscles at 48 hpf, prior to the onset of jaw movements.
source: Dual-expressing scxa/sox9a+ cells localize to cartilage attachment sites of cranial muscles at 48 hpf, prior to the onset of jaw movements (Figure 1A–D), consistent with specification of enthesis progenitors before the tendons or their skeletal muscle attachments become functional.
evidence: This is supported by the diagrams in Figure 1A-D showing cell localization.

claim: ShinyGO identified DEGs associated with 52 different pathways with FDR <0.05, including TGF-β, MAPK, Wnt, and Notch signaling, along with cell–cell adhesion and cell–ECM adhesion.
source: ShinyGO identified DEGs associated with 52 different pathways with FDR <0.05, including TGF-β, MAPK, Wnt, and Notch signaling, along with cell–cell adhesion and cell–ECM adhesion (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the pathway analysis results in Supplementary file 2.

claim: matn1 was the top-most upregulated gene in the RNA-seq analysis.
source: The top-most upregulated gene was matn1, which encodes an ECM protein highly enriched in cartilage; Matn1 enhances chondrogenesis of synovial fibroblasts treated with TGF-β (Pei et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data and a citation about Matn1 function.

claim: Matn1 enhances chondrogenesis of synovial fibroblasts treated with TGF-β.
source: The top-most upregulated gene was matn1, which encodes an ECM protein highly enriched in cartilage; Matn1 enhances chondrogenesis of synovial fibroblasts treated with TGF-β (Pei et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: klf2a was strongly upregulated in the RNA-seq analysis.
source: The transcription factor klf2a was also strongly upregulated; Klf2 and Klf4 have been implicated in enthesis development in mammalian tendons.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data.

claim: Klf2 and Klf4 have been implicated in enthesis development in mammalian tendons.
source: The transcription factor klf2a was also strongly upregulated; Klf2 and Klf4 have been implicated in enthesis development in mammalian tendons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Klf proteins in tendon development.

claim: Klf proteins repress TGF-β signaling in endothelial cells.
source: Klf proteins also repress TGF-β signaling in endothelial cells (Boon et al., 2007; Li et al., 2021) and klf2a expression is mechanosensitive during heart valve development (Steed et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: klf2a expression is mechanosensitive during heart valve development.
source: Klf proteins also repress TGF-β signaling in endothelial cells (Boon et al., 2007; Li et al., 2021) and klf2a expression is mechanosensitive during heart valve development (Steed et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: mxra5b encodes an ECM protein expressed in both tendons and ligaments during chick development.
source: The third DEG of particular interest was mxra5b, which encodes an ECM protein expressed in both tendons and ligaments during chick development (Robins and Capehart, 2018) and regulated by TGF-β in cultured human kidney epithelial cells (Poveda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: mxra5b is regulated by TGF-β in cultured human kidney epithelial cells.
source: The third DEG of particular interest was mxra5b, which encodes an ECM protein expressed in both tendons and ligaments during chick development (Robins and Capehart, 2018) and regulated by TGF-β in cultured human kidney epithelial cells (Poveda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Conventional chromogenic ISH for matn1 detected no expression at 36 hpf but very strong expression at 48 and 60 hpf in developing craniofacial and pectoral fin cartilages.
source: Conventional chromogenic ISH for matn1 detected no expression at 36 hpf but very strong expression at 48 and 60 hpf in developing craniofacial and pectoral fin cartilages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the ISH images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: scxa/matn1 co-expressing cells localized to the intermandibularis anterior tendon (ima) and sternohyoid tendon (sht), specifically in the entheses at 72 hpf.
source: scxa/matn1 co-expressing cells localized to the intermandibularis anterior tendon (ima) and sternohyoid tendon (sht), specifically in the entheses that attach to meckels, anterior edge of the ceratohyal cartilages, and the posterior enthesis of the ceratohyal (ch-pqt), at 72 hpf (Figure 2A–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by the isHCR images in Figure 2A–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: Chromogenic ISH revealed klf2a expression at VMS (somite boundaries) in the trunk at 48 hpf as well as developing pharyngeal arches and pectoral fins at 48 and 60 hpf.
source: For klf2a, chromogenic ISH revealed expression at VMS (somite boundaries) in the trunk at 48 hpf as well as developing pharyngeal arches and pectoral fins at 48 and 60 hpf (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by the ISH images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: Double isHCR of klf2a and scxa showed overlapping expression in tenocytes at VMS at 48 hpf.
source: This was confirmed by double isHCR of klf2a and scxa showing overlapping expression in tenocytes at VMS at 48 hpf (Figure 2G–J).
evidence: This is supported by the isHCR images in Figure 2G–J.

claim: klf2a expression was detected in multiple cranial tendons at 72 hpf, most prominently in the entheses of the ima, sht, and ch-pqt.
source: klf2a expression was also detected in multiple cranial tendons at 72 hpf, most prominantly in the entheses of the ima, sht, and ch-pqt (Figure 2K–P).
evidence: This is supported by the isHCR images in Figure 2K–P.

claim: mxra5b expression was first detected by chromogenic ISH at VMS near the horizontal myoseptum (HMS) at 36 hpf, as well as in the notochord and cranial mesenchyme at 48 hpf.
source: mxra5b expression was first detected by chromogenic ISH at VMS near the horizontal myoseptum (HMS), which separates dorsal and ventral somites at 36 hpf, as well as in the notochord and cranial mesenchyme at 48 hpf (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is supported by the ISH images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: Double isHCR for scxa and mxra5b detected mxra5b expression in cranial entheses and in the mandibulohyoid junction tendon (mhj) at 72 hpf.
source: Double isHCR for scxa and mxra5b, detected mxra5b expression in cranial entheses (including ima, mhj, and sht – as well as others not shown), and in the mandibulohyoid junction tendon (mhj) in embryos at 72 hpf (Figure 2Q–V).
evidence: This is supported by the isHCR images in Figure 2Q–V.

claim: At 48 hpf, all three genes (matn1, klf2a, mxra5b) were downregulated in cacnb1−/− mutants versus WT.
source: At 48 hpf, all three genes were downregulated in cacnb1−/− mutants versus WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the RT-qPCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At 72 hpf, only matn1 and mxra5b remained downregulated in cacnb1−/− embryos while klf2a expression increased.
source: In contrast, at 72 hpf once jaw movements had begun, only matn1 and mxra5b remained downregulated in cacnb1−/− embryos while klf2a expression increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the RT-qPCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Bulk RNA-seq of sorted mCherry+ cells from aBTX-injected embryos at 48 hpf compared with WT uninjected controls identified 1450 DEGs.
source: Bulk RNA-seq of sorted mCherry+ cells from whole aBTX-injected embryos at 48 hpf compared with WT uninjected controls (Figure 3A) identified 1450 DEGs.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 280 DEGs overlapped between the 36 vs 48 hpf bulk RNA-seq and the WT vs aBTX bulk RNA-seq experiments.
source: 280 DEGs overlapped between both bulk RNA-seq runs (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by the Venn diagram in Figure 3C.

claim: GO term analysis identified pathways such as 'Focal Adhesion', including rhoab, rock2a (both part of Rho-ROCK signaling), and col9a1a.
source: GO term analysis, using shinyGO (Ge et al., 2020), identified many of the same pathways downregulated in cacnb1−/− embryos, as well as others not previously implicated in tendon mechanotransduction. Seveal of these mapped to terms such as 'Focal Adhesion', including rhoab, rock2a (both part of Rho-ROCK signaling), and col9a1a (Figure 3E, Supplementary file 6) further implicating these as force dependent in tendons.
evidence: This is supported by the pathway analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: matn1 and mxra5b expression were both consistently downregulated by paralysis across multiple experiments.
source: Further, comparing the 48 hpf WT versus cacnb1−/− mutant RT-qPCR with both bulk RNA-seq experiments, matn1 and mxra5b expression were both consistently downregulated by paralysis, while klf2a expression was more variable across experiments (Figure 3A, D).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data across Figures 3A and 3D.

claim: klf2a expression was more variable across paralysis experiments.
source: Further, comparing the 48 hpf WT versus cacnb1−/− mutant RT-qPCR with both bulk RNA-seq experiments, matn1 and mxra5b expression were both consistently downregulated by paralysis, while klf2a expression was more variable across experiments (Figure 3A, D).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data across Figures 3A and 3D.

claim: At 48 hpf, RT-qPCR revealed significant global downregulation of matn1 and mxra5b in αBTX paralyzed embryos compared to WT uninjected siblings.
source: At 48 hpf, RT-qPCR revealed significant global downregulation of matn1 and mxra5b in αBTX paralyzed embryos compared to WT uninjected siblings, like cacnb1−/− mutant embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) and were upregulated in aBTX-T and aBTX-R embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the RT-qPCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: matn1 and mxra5b were upregulated in aBTX-T (twitching) and aBTX-R (recovered) embryos.
source: At 48 hpf, RT-qPCR revealed significant global downregulation of matn1 and mxra5b in αBTX paralyzed embryos compared to WT uninjected siblings, like cacnb1−/− mutant embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) and were upregulated in aBTX-T and aBTX-R embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the RT-qPCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: klf2a was upregulated in paralyzed embryos, though this increase was not statistically significant from WT controls.
source: In contrast, klf2a was upregulated in paralyzed embryos, though this increase was also not statistically significant from WT controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the RT-qPCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In ima tenocytes, there was no significant difference in matn1 expression between WT and paralyzed embryos.
source: In these ima tenocytes, we found no significant difference in matn1 expression between WT and paralyzed embryos, but increased expression in fully recovered (aBTX-R) embryos relative to WT, Paralyzed, and Twitching (aBTX-T) embryos (Figure 4U).
evidence: This is supported by the quantification in Figure 4U.

claim: matn1 expression increased in fully recovered (aBTX-R) embryos relative to WT, Paralyzed, and Twitching (aBTX-T) embryos in ima tenocytes.
source: In these ima tenocytes, we found no significant difference in matn1 expression between WT and paralyzed embryos, but increased expression in fully recovered (aBTX-R) embryos relative to WT, Paralyzed, and Twitching (aBTX-T) embryos (Figure 4U).
evidence: This is supported by the quantification in Figure 4U.

claim: Tenocytes of the sht enthesis showed no significant difference in matn1 expression across any of the force conditions.
source: Conversely, tenocytes of the sht enthesis showed no significant difference in expression across any of the conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1M).
evidence: This is supported by the quantification in Figure 4—figure supplement 1M.

claim: mxra5b expression in the ima enthesis was significantly reduced in paralyzed, aBTX-T twitching, and remained low in aBTX-R fully recovered embryos compared to WT.
source: mxra5b expression in the ima enthesis was significantly reduced in paralyzed, aBTX-T twitching, and remained low in aBTX-R fully recovered embryos compared to WT (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Z).
evidence: This is supported by the quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 1Z.

claim: In tenocytes of all other measured attachment sites (sht enthesis, mhj MTJ, sht MTJ), mxra5b expression returned to WT levels upon full recovery.
source: However, in tenocytes of all other measured attachment sites (sht enthesis, mhj MTJ, sht MTJ), mxra5b expression returned to WT levels upon full recovery (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 2M, Figure 5—figure supplement 3M).
evidence: This is supported by the quantifications in Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 2M, and Figure 5—figure supplement 3M.

claim: klf2a expression in ima and sht entheses was significantly increased in paralyzed and aBTX-T embryos compared to WT and further increased upon full recovery.
source: klf2a expression in ima and sht entheses was significantly increased in paralyzed and aBTX-T embryos compared to WT and further increased upon full recovery (Figure 4—figure supplement 1Z, Figure 5—figure supplement 1M).
evidence: This is supported by the quantifications in Figure 4—figure supplement 1Z and Figure 5—figure supplement 1M.

claim: klf2a expression in sht MTJ tenocytes only increased significantly from twitching to full recovery.
source: However, unlike entheses, klf2a expression in sht MTJ tenocytes only increased significantly from twitching to full recovery, and in mhj MTJ tenocytes the pattern was much more variable, increasing upon paralysis, decreasing to WT levels at twitching, and re-increasing beyond WT levels at full recovery (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Figure 6U).
evidence: This is supported by the quantifications in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Figure 6U.

claim: In mhj MTJ tenocytes, klf2a expression increased upon paralysis, decreased to WT levels at twitching, and re-increased beyond WT levels at full recovery.
source: However, unlike entheses, klf2a expression in sht MTJ tenocytes only increased significantly from twitching to full recovery, and in mhj MTJ tenocytes the pattern was much more variable, increasing upon paralysis, decreasing to WT levels at twitching, and re-increasing beyond WT levels at full recovery (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Figure 6U).
evidence: This is supported by the quantifications in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Figure 6U.

claim: Tg(scxa:mCherry) embryos injected with four mxra5b gRNAs had qualitatively fewer trunk tenocytes when compared to uninjected controls.
source: While we did not observe obvious phenotypic defects in matn1 and klf2a CRISPants, possibly due to genetic redundancy with other similar proteins, Tg(scxa:mCherry) embryos injected with four mxra5b gRNAs had qualitatively fewer trunk tenocytes when compared to uninjected controls (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by the images in Figure 7A.

claim: Trunk VMS in mxra5b CRISPR-injected embryos displayed a wider sb angle.
source: Additionally, trunk VMS in mxra5b CRISPR-injected embryos displayed a wider sb angle (Figure 7B), although this may reflect a role for mxra5b in the notochord, where it is also expressed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G–I).
evidence: This is supported by the quantification in Figure 7B.

claim: mxra5b may be required for embryonic axial tenocyte migration and/or differentiation.
source: These results suggest that mxra5b may be required for embryonic axial tenocyte migration and/or differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the CRISPR phenotype data.

claim: Cells with distinct enthesis or MTJ signatures arise in the embryo to fine-tune the ECM to match the functional demands of and forces exerted by individual muscles.
source: In contrast to classical studies of mature tendons these results suggest that cells with distinct enthesis or MTJ signatures arise in the embryo to fine-tune the ECM to match the functional demands of and forces exerted by individual muscles.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential gene expression patterns observed across different tendon types.

claim: matn1 and its relatives have been reported in single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) analyses of adult tenocytes and fibrocartilage.
source: Though typically thought of as cartilage-specific, matn1 and its relatives have been reported in single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) analyses of adult tenocytes and fibrocartilage (Kaji et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: matn1 transcription is upregulated upon mechanical load in cultured chondrocytes.
source: They are also consistent with studies showing that matn1 transcription is upregulated upon mechanical load in cultured chondrocytes (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Chondrocyte ECM becomes disorganized in Matn1−/− mutant mice exposed to mechanical loads after medial meniscus destabilization surgery.
source: Chondrocyte ECM becomes disorganized in Matn1−/− mutant mice exposed to mechanical loads after medial meniscus destabilization surgery (Chen et al., 2016; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mxra5 (also known as adlican) encodes a secreted proteoglycan implicated in cell–cell adhesion and ECM remodeling, mainly in the context of colorectal and other cancers.
source: Mxra5 (also known as adlican) encodes a secreted proteoglycan implicated in cell–cell adhesion and ECM remodeling, mainly in the context of colorectal and other cancers (He et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mxra5 is expressed in tendons and other connective tissues of developing chick embryos as well as human fibroblasts.
source: Mxra5 is expressed in tendons and other connective tissues of developing chick embryos as well as human fibroblasts (Chondrogianni et al., 2004; Robins and Capehart, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MXRA5 is inhibited by TGF-β1.
source: Consistent with a force-responsive gene, MXRA5 is inhibited by TGF-β1 (Poveda et al., 2017), and associated with migration of dental pulp stem cells (Yoshida et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: MXRA5 is associated with migration of dental pulp stem cells.
source: Consistent with a force-responsive gene, MXRA5 is inhibited by TGF-β1 (Poveda et al., 2017), and associated with migration of dental pulp stem cells (Yoshida et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Klf2-binding sites have been identified upstream of ECM genes such as Col5 in sorted entheseal tenocytes.
source: Klf2-binding sites have been identified upstream of ECM genes such as Col5 in sorted entheseal tenocytes (Kult et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Klf2 expression is upregulated by fluid forces in endocardial cells leading to fibronectin synthesis.
source: Klf2 expression is also upregulated by fluid forces in endocardial cells leading to fibronectin synthesis (Boselli et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2006; Steed et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The bulk RNA-seq analysis identifies new regulators of tenocyte–ECM, going beyond the better studied collagens.
source: Together, our bulk RNA-seq analysis of embryonic zebrafish tenocytes and their transcriptional responses to muscle contraction: (1) identifies new regulators of tenocyte–ECM, going beyond the better studied collagens, and (2) highlights the importance of considering developmental events that specify the mechanical properties of tendons as they form.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The bulk RNA-seq analysis highlights the importance of considering developmental events that specify the mechanical properties of tendons as they form.
source: Together, our bulk RNA-seq analysis of embryonic zebrafish tenocytes and their transcriptional responses to muscle contraction: (1) identifies new regulators of tenocyte–ECM, going beyond the better studied collagens, and (2) highlights the importance of considering developmental events that specify the mechanical properties of tendons as they form.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Trunk tenocytes in zebrafish undergo dramatic morphological transformations when muscle contractions begin.
source: We previously showed that trunk tenocytes in zebrafish undergo dramatic morphological transformations when muscle contractions begin (Subramanian et al., 2018; Subramanian et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Morphological changes in tenocytes occur when embryos transition from twitching (36 hpf) to free-swimming behaviors (48 hpf).
source: These occur when embryos transition from twitching (36 hr post-fertilization, hpf) to free-swimming behaviors (48 hpf), as well as between sporadic jaw contractions at 60 hpf, and free-feeding behavior at 72 hpf (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by the diagrams in Figure 1A–D.

claim: Morphological changes in tenocytes occur between sporadic jaw contractions at 60 hpf and free-feeding behavior at 72 hpf.
source: These occur when embryos transition from twitching (36 hr post-fertilization, hpf) to free-swimming behaviors (48 hpf), as well as between sporadic jaw contractions at 60 hpf, and free-feeding behavior at 72 hpf (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by the diagrams in Figure 1A–D.

claim: The Tg(scxa:mCherry) line predominantly labels both embryonic trunk and cranial tenocytes.
source: The Tg(scxa:mCherry) line predominantly labels both embryonic trunk and cranial tenocytes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the transgenic line used.

claim: GO analysis for Biological Process terms associated with the top DEGs showed significant enrichment for 'skeletal system development' and 'ECM organization'.
source: GO analysis for Biological Process terms associated with the top DEGs showed significant enrichment for 'skeletal system development' and 'ECM organization' (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by the GO analysis results shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Recent single-cell sequencing studies of enthesis lineage trajectories in mice support the specification of enthesis progenitors before tendons become functional.
source: These results also fit with recent single-cell sequencing studies of enthesis lineage trajectories in mice (Fang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: This study provides the first evidence for klf2a as an enthesis marker in craniofacial tendons.
source: This provides the first evidence for klf2a as an enthesis marker in craniofacial tendons, similar to Klf2 expression in developing mouse limb entheses (Kult et al., 2021; Lu and Thomopoulos, 2013; Zelzer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a novel finding from the current study, supported by comparison to previous work in mice.

claim: mxra5b expression has not been described in cranial connective tissues previously.
source: Similar to klf2a, mxra5b expression has not been described in cranial connective tissues previously.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the current study.

claim: This study reports the first genome-wide survey of embryonic mechanoresponsive genes and transcriptional responses across multiple tendon types.
source: We report the first genome-wide survey of embryonic mechanoresponsive genes and transcriptional responses across multiple tendon types.
evidence: This is a summary of the novelty of the current study.

claim: This study identifies three genes (matn1, mxra5b, klf2a) induced at the onset of muscle contraction and later maintained by contractile force.
source: We identify three genes induced at the onset of muscle attraction and later maintained by contractile force (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings, supported by Figure 8A.

claim: Paralysis of zebrafish embryos alters expression of two ECM proteins in tenocytes, matn1 and mxra5b, as well as the transcription factor klf2a.
source: Paralysis of zebrafish embryos alters expression of two ECM proteins in tenocytes, matn1 and mxra5b, as well as the transcription factor klf2a.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the paralysis experiments.

claim: All three genes (matn1, mxra5b, klf2a) are expressed in cranial entheses.
source: All three are expressed in cranial entheses, while mxra5b and klf2a are also expressed in trunk MTJs (Figure 2, Figure 8B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the isHCR data in Figure 2 and related supplementary figures.

claim: mxra5b and klf2a are also expressed in trunk MTJs.
source: All three are expressed in cranial entheses, while mxra5b and klf2a are also expressed in trunk MTJs (Figure 2, Figure 8B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the isHCR data in Figure 2 and related supplementary figures.

claim: Embryonic tenocytes in zebrafish acquire specialized morphologies and gene expression profiles as muscles first form functional attachments.
source: Our previous studies have shown that in both tissues embryonic tenocytes in zebrafish acquire specialized morphologies and gene expression profiles as muscles first form functional attachments (Subramanian et al., 2018; Subramanian et al., 2023; Subramanian and Schilling, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Tendon types and subdomains are distinguished by their collagen composition.
source: Classically tendon types and subdomains are distinguished by their collagen composition, and many collagens are direct Scx or Mkx transcriptional targets (Bobzin et al., 2021; Felsenthal and Zelzer, 2017; Subramanian and Schilling, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Many collagens are direct Scx or Mkx transcriptional targets.
source: Classically tendon types and subdomains are distinguished by their collagen composition, and many collagens are direct Scx or Mkx transcriptional targets (Bobzin et al., 2021; Felsenthal and Zelzer, 2017; Subramanian and Schilling, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The gradient of stiffness within an enthesis corresponds to a gradient of Scx/Sox9 expression.
source: This helps explain the gradient of stiffness and corresponding Scx/Sox9 expression within an enthesis (Blitz et al., 2013; Lu and Thomopoulos, 2013; Subramanian et al., 2023; Zelzer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Zebrafish matn1 regulation differs between entheses that form at different stages.
source: We find that zebrafish matn1 regulation differs between entheses that form at different stages (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative isHCR data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Paralyzed embryos at both twitching and swimming stages show reduced tenocyte matn1 expression.
source: Whereas paralyzed embryos at both twitching and swimming stages show reduced tenocyte matn1 expression (Figure 3D), our isHCR data reveal that expression only rebounds after full recovery of muscle contraction in the ima enthesis (Figure 8B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data in Figure 3D and isHCR data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: matn1 expression only rebounds after full recovery of muscle contraction in the ima enthesis.
source: Whereas paralyzed embryos at both twitching and swimming stages show reduced tenocyte matn1 expression (Figure 3D), our isHCR data reveal that expression only rebounds after full recovery of muscle contraction in the ima enthesis (Figure 8B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the isHCR data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: These spatial and temporal differences in matn1 expression support the hypothesis that these are bona fide embryonic entheseal tenocytes specified at the edges of cartilages as muscles first attach.
source: These spatial and temporal differences support our hypothesis that these are bona fide embryonic entheseal tenocytes specified at the edges of cartilages as muscles first attach (Subramanian et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: This study provides the first evidence for regulation of mxra5b transcription in tenocytes by mechanotransduction.
source: Our results provide the first evidence for regulation of mxra5b transcription in tenocytes by mechanotransduction.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the current study.

claim: In the ima enthesis, paralysis downregulates mxra5b expression, with little rebound after recovery.
source: For example, in the ima enthesis, paralysis downregulates mxra5b expression, with little rebound after recovery (Figure 8B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative isHCR data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: At other entheses and MTJs, mxra5b expression returns to WT levels upon full recovery after paralysis.
source: In contrast, at other entheses and MTJs mxra5b expression returns to WT levels upon full recovery after paralysis (Figures 5 and 8, Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative isHCR data in Figure 5 and related supplementary figures.

claim: mxra5b expression may require continuous mechanical activation, levels of which differ between tendons as well as entheses or MTJs.
source: mxra5b expression may require continuous mechanical activation, levels of which differ between tendons as well as entheses or MTJs (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential expression patterns observed across different tendon types and force conditions.

claim: Zebrafish klf2a expression localizes to embryonic cranial entheses.
source: Similar to matn1 and mxra5b, (1) zebrafish klf2a expression localizes to embryonic cranial entheses, (2) its transcription increases in tenocytes at the onset of muscle contraction, and (3) these responses vary between spatially distinct tendons and tendon subdomains (Figure 8B, Figure 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 3, Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by the isHCR data in multiple figures.

claim: klf2a transcription increases in tenocytes at the onset of muscle contraction.
source: Similar to matn1 and mxra5b, (1) zebrafish klf2a expression localizes to embryonic cranial entheses, (2) its transcription increases in tenocytes at the onset of muscle contraction, and (3) these responses vary between spatially distinct tendons and tendon subdomains (Figure 8B, Figure 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 3, Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq and isHCR data in multiple figures.

claim: klf2a responses to force vary between spatially distinct tendons and tendon subdomains.
source: Similar to matn1 and mxra5b, (1) zebrafish klf2a expression localizes to embryonic cranial entheses, (2) its transcription increases in tenocytes at the onset of muscle contraction, and (3) these responses vary between spatially distinct tendons and tendon subdomains (Figure 8B, Figure 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 3, Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative isHCR data in multiple figures.

claim: Cranial tenocytes in zebrafish upregulate klf2a upon recovery from paralysis.
source: Cranial tenocytes in zebrafish upregulate klf2a upon recovery from paralysis (Figures 3 and 6, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 3), though there are discrepancies between isHCR, bulk RNA-seq, and RT-qPCR measurements.
evidence: This is supported by data in multiple figures, though with noted discrepancies between methods.

claim: There are discrepancies between isHCR, bulk RNA-seq, and RT-qPCR measurements of klf2a expression.
source: Cranial tenocytes in zebrafish upregulate klf2a upon recovery from paralysis (Figures 3 and 6, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 3), though there are discrepancies between isHCR, bulk RNA-seq, and RT-qPCR measurements.
evidence: This is acknowledged based on comparison of data from different experimental methods.

claim: Discrepancies in klf2a measurements may reflect the fact that klf2a is also expressed in other tissues, such as embryonic vascular and endocardial cells.
source: These may reflect the fact that klf2a is also expressed in other tissues, such as embryonic vascular and endocardial cells (Figure 2; Goddard et al., 2017) or differences in expression between trunk and cranial tenocyte populations.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern shown in Figure 2 and supported by a citation.

claim: Discrepancies in klf2a measurements may reflect differences in expression between trunk and cranial tenocyte populations.
source: These may reflect the fact that klf2a is also expressed in other tissues, such as embryonic vascular and endocardial cells (Figure 2; Goddard et al., 2017) or differences in expression between trunk and cranial tenocyte populations.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed differences in expression patterns.

claim: Force-dependent klf2a expression may be critical for tissue-specific ECM remodeling in many contexts.
source: Thus, force-dependent klf2a expression may be critical for tissue-specific ECM remodeling in many contexts.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and previous knowledge about Klf2 function.

claim: The presence of matn1, mxra5b, and klf2a in embryonic tendons and their responses to force during normal development versus recovery from paralysis raises questions as to whether the mechanisms that initially establish these structures differ from those that control their maintenance.
source: The presence of these genes in embryonic tendons and their responses to force during normal development versus recovery from paralysis raises questions as to whether the mechanisms that initially establish these structures differ from those that control their maintenance (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed differences in gene expression patterns.

claim: Understanding specific tenocyte–ECM interactions will require novel approaches to measuring the effect of varying ECM microenvironment protein compositions on tenocyte gene expression.
source: Given the large variation of cell–ECM feedback mechanisms throughout embryonic development, understanding specific tenocyte–ECM interactions will require novel approaches to measuring the effect of varying (1) ECM microenvironment protein compositions, or local 'matrisomes', on tenocyte gene expression and (2) intrinsic gene expression patterns of heterogeneous tenocyte populations spatially and functionally.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: Understanding specific tenocyte–ECM interactions will require novel approaches to measuring intrinsic gene expression patterns of heterogeneous tenocyte populations spatially and functionally.
source: Given the large variation of cell–ECM feedback mechanisms throughout embryonic development, understanding specific tenocyte–ECM interactions will require novel approaches to measuring the effect of varying (1) ECM microenvironment protein compositions, or local 'matrisomes', on tenocyte gene expression and (2) intrinsic gene expression patterns of heterogeneous tenocyte populations spatially and functionally.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: Single-cell approaches (e.g. scRNA-seq) at different developmental stages and in the presence or absence of force will provide a clearer understanding of how individual spatially and functionally distinct tenocyte populations respond to force in development.
source: Single-cell approaches (e.g. scRNA-seq) at different developmental stages and in the presence or absence of force, will provide a clearer understanding of how individual spatially and functionally distinct tenocyte populations respond to force in development.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: Integrating knowledge of the basic biology of tenocytes at multiple scales will be essential for developing a better picture of tenocyte–ECM interactions at individual tendons.
source: Integrating such knowledge of the basic biology of tenocytes at multiple scales will be essential for developing a better picture of tenocyte–ECM interactions at individual tendons, paving the path to advance personalized translational therapies for tendon injuries.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the implications of the research.
